abstract: A directed strongly regular graph with parameters $(v, k, t, \lambda, \mu)$ is defined by a quadratic identity for its adjacency matrix. The first survey reduced the 38 early papers of the rStation problem on such graphs to fifteen general theorems; this survey covers the next 113 papers on parameter sets of the Hobart–Brouwer table. We reduce the common steps of these papers to theorems with complete proofs in uniform notation. The constructions rest on gluing in an eigenvalue pencil, a layered form over an arbitrary group, an orbit model, graphs on copies and switching of sign matrices. The obstructions rest on the trace of an automorphism of any order, the structure of the set of fixed vertices, the rank of the quotient modulo the order of an automorphism, a transfer identity under which the two lines of twins are complements of each other, a maximum principle for the column space of $A + I$ when $t = \lambda + 1$, and a frequency decomposition of the skew-symmetric part on closed sets. The theorems give short derivations of known results: the series $(mc^2, 2mc - 1, m(c + 2) - 1, m(c + 2) - 2, 2m)$ with odd $c$ is excluded by a single identity, and a hypothetical graph $(98, 20, 9, 8, 3)$ has least mass 21 of a nonzero nonnegative integer vector in the column space of $A + I$. A computation by the symmetry theorems excludes an automorphism of order 5 for $(88, 18, 12, 2, 4)$, which is a new result, and independently confirms the same for $(88, 9, 3, 0, 1)$. Every paper of the corpus is assigned to a section or excluded with a reason, and computations that are claimed but not recomputed are marked.
author: meleta
change_summary: Version 2 answers the seven comments of the review of version 1. The corrections state the hypotheses of Theorems 3.1(d) and 5.1(b) exactly, compare Theorems 4.1 and 7.1 with the literature, and recount the census over the pairs that are open by published status; no result on a parameter set has changed. (1) Section 7, the introduction and Table 11.1 compare Theorem 7.1 with Theorem 2.3 of De Winter, Kamischke and Wang [122]: the trace identities for an automorphism of any order are their result, item (b) is the DSRG analogue of Corollary 2.2 of paper [122], and our formulation is item (c): it expresses the multiplicities through the dimensions of the fixed subspaces of subgroups and is therefore checked from the numbers of fixed vertices and of arcs x → hx of the powers of the automorphism. Section 2 now derives that every DSRG has μ ≥ 1, so the analogue of Corollary 2.2 of paper [122] holds for every DSRG. The number [122] now belongs to this paper; paper 153 of the problem, which was [122] in version 1, is now [123]. (2) The spectrum and the multiplicities in Theorem 4.1 are no longer called new: they are the standard decomposition of the regular representation from the proof of item (a). (3) Table 11.2 separates the published status of a pair from our check. The pair (81, 48, 32, 26, 32) is recorded as solved: paper [78] proved its nonexistence, and we have not recomputed the computation of the paper. Section 12 states the rule, the published status, as in the first survey, and the pairs of the census of Section 7 are selected by the same rule: there are 264 of them instead of 266, because (81, 32, 16, 15, 11) and (90, 38, 20, 16, 16) are solved as well; Sections 8 and 12 treat the pair H_1(9) by the same rule. The numbers of the census are recomputed: Theorem 7.3 removes 406 prime orders from 171 pairs; the list of pairs and the records of the supplement are rebuilt. (4) Theorem 5.1(b) gives the quadratic identity for all a, b, and a DSRG for j ≥ 2 exactly when a + b > 0; the example for a = b = 0 is the triangular graph T(5) with set (10, 6, 6, 3, 4); the copy without arcs is excluded. (5) Theorem 3.1(d) and Corollary 3.3 explicitly require crossed blocks, speak of the equalities (1) with μ ≥ 1, and give a DSRG only for 0 < M − rs < K from the definition of a DSRG; the proof of Theorem 3.4(b) checks this inequality. (6) The proof of Corollary 6.3 no longer assumes that a switched graph has constant row sums: it rests on the fact that switching preserves the absence of a sign vector (Theorem 6.1(d)) and on Theorem 6.1(c). The beginning of Section 6.2 says that S² = −6S + 27I holds for the graphs with set O_p and for the complements of the graphs with set E_p, while for the graphs with set E_p themselves α = 6. (7) Theorem 10.3(b) takes δ = r − s = √Δ > 0 from the notation of the section.
title: DSRG in 113 papers of the rStation problem: general theorems on constructions, symmetry and nonexistence
